https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Laurence Fox on his anti-woke party, racism rows and why he needs a bodyguard
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Across Laurence Fox’s open-plan sitting room, I glimpse the future. It’s possibly, although one hopes not, the future of British politics. Almost unavoidably, it is the future of Laurence, the well-loved scion of the Fox acting dynasty who has recast himself as the leader of the anti-woke brigade’s brand new party.
At first I think the huge bloke I spot in his kitchen must be our photographer, so I call out that I am wrapping up the interview. He looks puzzled. That’s no snapper. That’s Fox’s bodyguard.
“Paul keeps an eye on me,” Fox explains. “He makes sure no one throws a punch.”
Is he is joking?
“No, there are some nasty people out there.”
And the party pays for Paul?
“The party has a budget and within that budget is a budget for security. Of course there is. Do you want a milkshake in your face? I don’t particularly. I certainly don’t want any violence anywhere near my children [he has two sons from his marriage to Billie Piper]. Their wellbeing is absolutely 100 per cent my thing.”
It has been a year of two halves for Laurence Fox. At its beginning, the 42-year-old, who for a decade was the temperate James Hathaway in ITV’s Lewis, managed to accuse a black woman of racism on television, a bon mot that sank his acting career in spectacularly speedy fashion. In April his mother died. Then in September came what he must regard as, and I rather doubt can be, the good news. Just as his fans had got used to him playing Lord Palmerston in Victoria, he became a politician for real and leader of the Reclaim Party. Although still awaiting the Electoral Commission’s approval for its name, Reclaim has registered “interest” from 30,000 visitors to its rudimentary website and has lined its pockets with a £5 million donation from Jeremy Hosking, a right-wing businessman who approached Fox with this new wheeze in the summer.
Our conversation starts in the kitchen of his recently bought terraced house in Stockwell, south London. Its very atmosphere is politically incorrect, filled with tobacco smoke generated by Fox and two Reclaim PRs. He wants me to view on his phone a clip from Channel 5’s Jeremy Vine show in which the journalist Yasmin Alibhai-Brown calls him “a racist bully”. He is trying to work out whether her immediate retraction, unaccompanied by the “formal apology” he asked for, precludes him from suing. For someone who has been through a messy divorce, he seems curiously keen for some more learned friends to re-enter his already complicated life.
For our discussion, we sit in his front room drinking coffee, in my case from a mug marked LIBERAL TEARS: STILL WARM. He takes his coffee with more roll-ups, of which he reckons he gets through 30 a day, resulting in a voice that sounds as if it has trundled up a mineshaft. At one point his dogs, Blaze the labrador and Sparky the Jack Russell, get excited and he commands them to leave. I praise their obedience.
“Well, you know, you’ve got to have a pack leader with dogs. Otherwise dogs bark and they’re noisy and they’re not polite to guests. Dogs are like anyone. They need to understand good manners, don’t they?”
Does Britain need a strong leader then, I ask, my mind flashing up an image of Oswald Mosley in his Seventies fantasy comeback phase.
“Britain needs a leader, yes, someone who doesn’t flip-flop between one thing or the other, and someone with deep conviction and a patriotic love for this land of ours. Absolutely it does. Look at the mess we’re in at the moment.”
Does modesty forbid him from naming that man?
“I don’t know who that man is.”
Is it him?
“No. At the moment, no,” he says, ominously.
We go back a dozen years, Laurence and I, and given how much else has changed for him, I am surprised how little he has physically altered: his hair still, perhaps suspiciously, blond, his face still fresh and smooth. The first time I interviewed him, in 2008, was soon after his marriage to Piper, the former pop singer turned actress, at their Withnail-like cottage in Sussex. With typical acuity I judged the girl from the Swindon state school and the Old Harrovian well suited, “funny, clever, their work ethic checked by a slacker tendency”. Three years later, I met him for Lewis in Oxford, where Fox was fishing for pike in the Isis. He remembers telling me he was bored. Four years after that, we were in a pub in London discussing his new album — he is a part-time singer-songwriter — which seemed largely to be about his rows with Piper. “Yeah,” he says now, “it was really going tits-up then when we spoke.” The following year, 2016, they divorced.
In all these encounters I would never have thought him a reactionary. He was anti private schools, not wishing his boys to turn out “posh” — a “leftie” position he retains, although he lost the argument with Piper. Winston, 12, and Eugene, 8, go to “expensive, progressive private” schools. Playing De Gaulle in a play four years ago, he refused to say the word “mongol” in relation to the French president’s daughter with Down’s syndrome. He weirdly voted for Jeremy Corbyn in 2017.
So has he changed or has the world?
“No, I’ve stayed the same.” It is the moral superiority of the left that has altered, he explains. “You are cancelled and removed from this society and this culture unless you hold a certain set of views,” he says, although his views, not dissimilar to those readily available in the papers and online in any case, have been everywhere in the past nine months.
I agree that virtue signalling is irritating. Motives are hard to prove, and people do things to look good or because they feel guilty, but the result of it just may be a more egalitarian, fairer society.
“I couldn’t disagree with you more. I think we are the most divided we’ve ever been as a society. In my lifetime, it’s the most divided. I think identitarianism is poison, absolute utter poison.”
In the checklist of views that these days tells you on which side of cultural wars you lie, Fox’s opinions occupy almost exclusively the column on the right, the single exception being Brexit, where he stood, as he says, on the “virtuous” — that is the Remainer — side.
Race is his starter for ten. On BBC Question Time in January they were discussing the Duchess of Sussex’s drubbing in the press. From the audience, Rachel Boyle, an academic specialising in race, racism and ethnicity, said the abuse Meghan was attracting was racism. His head shaking wearily, Fox disagreed (“We are the most tolerant, lovely country in Europe”) and said her argument was getting “boring”. Boyle, who anyone could see is black, called him a “white privileged male”. He told her she was being racist towards him.
Was it sensible to call a black woman a racist?
“She was being racist. Yeah, I think we should call out individual examples of racism.”
But we know racism against white people doesn’t matter half as much as racism against black people.
“Why is that?”
Because we (I also opine as a white privileged male) have held the upper hand for centuries. Our feelings are pretty impregnable.
“Who ended slavery?” he asks.
We did, having promulgated it for centuries.
“Yes, but who ended it? All I’m asking for is, instead of going, ‘You’re all evil white people,’ to remember 1,500 British Royal Navy people died stopping slavery by the Barbary pirates.”
On the night, the QT chairwoman, Fiona Bruce, felt things were becoming unseemly and moved on. The row stayed put and got stuck in. Soon a committee of the actors’ union, Equity, had tweeted that Fox was a disgrace to his industry. Not long afterwards his agent, Sue Latimer, took him off her books.
There were other consequences. His girlfriend, the fashion designer and photographer, Sara McKinnon, who is half-Kuwaiti, dumped him (he denies reports they are back together). Relations with his sister, Lydia, and her husband, the comedian Richard Ayoade, who is half-Nigerian, became strained, although he now says he sees them all the time.
Initially, Fox appeared to stop digging the hole he was in. He met the academic Bonnie Greer and over coffee at the British Museum she explained how he had offended. On Twitter they posed in an embrace, although she has since, he says, failed to respond to his offers of more coffee. Today I discover his views on race have calcified into a political position. Yes, black people have had “historically a more difficult time”, he will say, but then triumphantly add that the pay gap between black and white people between 16 and 30 is now “non-existent”.
I point out that it will be non-existent in the lower-paid, less senior jobs. Higher up, including in my newsroom, black people are under-represented. He agrees there is more we can do, but says unless we point out the positive steps we have taken, our children will leave school thinking “we need to de-colonise the curriculum, we need to remove statues”.
But sinking Edward Colston’s statue in Bristol harbour was by popular demand and a good thing, I say.
“No, it’s appalling. It was absolutely wrong,” he says. “It’s not up to mobs to turn up and tear down statues.”
And on to Black Lives Matter. I admit the reaction to George Floyd’s killing was a wake-up call for me. The feelings of black people are now higher up my personal agenda. Whatever the additional political objectives of it, BLM has done the world a great deal of good. Does he agree?
“Of course black lives matter,” he says.
But the slogan exists because black people feel theirs don’t?
“We are addressing it. Are we not? But then, help us out here. Let’s also have a broad discussion about it. You notice how George Floyd has disappeared slightly into the background in terms of what’s happening in his legal case and the consequences surrounding his death.”
What does he mean by that?
“Well just, you know, the autopsy findings in regards to him and all of this stuff.”
Hang on. This sounds a bit conspiracy theorist. “No. Look it up and then we can discuss it,” he suggests.
“Black Lives Matter as a movement is there to topple western democracy and defund the family and defund law enforcement. And I’m sorry, I’m not happy about that. It’s like, sorry, no, I don’t agree with you as a movement. I stand in direct opposition to you as a movement because I take a more balanced view.”
And here come more of Fox’s more balanced views.
MeToo: “MeToo started in the black community in America. It didn’t start in the white showbiz community. It was interesting actually that showbusiness, the most hypocritical, casting couch-based system of female oppression — if there is such a thing, which is another conversation — decided to take it on. It gave it another layer of moral superiority and hypocrisy.”
The trans debate: “There are now 136 or something recognised genders. This isn’t science.”
The BBC: “Utterly defund the BBC, decriminalise the licence fee and get rid of it, throw it out to the free market.”
Extinction Rebellion: “Doomsday cultists have existed all over the world, haven’t they, for many, many years. And that’s fine. Is there man-made climate change? Of course there is. Is it the end of the world? No.”
The Covid-19 restrictions, which he cheerfully tweeted on November 29 he had ignored by holding a large lunch party: “I suppose we gave up our freedom so quickly because we were all so terrified, and that’s totally understandable. But how do you get that liberty back?”
The NHS — actually, there is a balance here. Its emergency care is “astonishingly good” as he discovered when his mother fell down some stairs. Covid, however, has proved it “unfit for purpose” and there was no clapping from him on Thursday nights.
“I just happen to wonder that if a virus of this level of survivability is going to overwhelm a hugely well-funded organisation then whether there is a problem with the management of that organisation.
“It’s the new God, you know,” says Fox, the son of evangelical Christians, who “most certainly” believes in God and prays with his children.
I tell him what it all sounds like to many people: were Laurence a child we would say he has got very angry and is now acting out and causing fights.
He takes this with equanimity and refers me to the theory of the Overton window of political acceptability. “If your Overton window is that far over there [his palms measure out a space to the left], there are many ways to bring it back to the centre and one of them is for you to give it a good shove, because it starts making conversation. I’m only really interested in generating conversations.”
But look at the conversations he is generating! He has got a respected Asian journalist calling him a racist.
“That probably says more about her than it does about me, I would say, seeing as I dealt with her [on Channel 5] in a very calm and generous and reasoned manner.”
He did, but he is also saying things, albeit in his calm, educated voice, so inflammatory that there’s a bodyguard in his kitchen. Fox throws the names of academics into our conversation, talks of “cognitive dissonance” and “critical race theory”, but much as he would like us to think he has locked himself in his study and read each side of every argument, his arguments sound as if they come from a position of aggrieved pain.
His hostility to the NHS sounds almost personal. Perhaps it is. He tells me graphically of a 55-year-old friend who “choked on their own vomit after not being put on a heart rate monitor in the NHS two weeks ago”. No, he is not suggesting NHS negligence. His mother, Mary, died at home in April because having worked in the NHS in her youth and being “a smart cookie”, she did not want to die in hospital. “Breaking the rules again,” her family were at her bedside. “She had multiple medical issues and she passed away but they were mad keen to put it down to a Covid death.” These stories sound angry, politicised.
Where he has a justifiable grievance is that his career has been killed because he spoke his mind in a free society. He is deeply hurt, as well he might be — his father is James Fox (star of that classic Sixties movie Performance, a poster of which is framed above his sofa); half of his family is in showbusiness. As he sees it, an agent who knows he is not racist dropped him because others said he was, and now he has no access to work.
“When something like that happens to you, emotionally it’s very profound – to have your career, 22 years of a career, just gone. Bye! So you have a visceral, emotional reaction to it, which makes you feel hopeless and broken, and then you start going, ‘God, there’s something really badly wrong here.’ And then you go, ‘I need to do something about it.’ That’s the process.”
Yet to believe 2020 remade Fox is to deny the continuity in the life of an extrovert from a noisy theatrical family that, despite its descent into religiosity, was bohemian, dissident and suspicious of institutions.
“We sat round dinner tables and we were encouraged to explore all our views and to speak freely, and, as you know, that got me into trouble at Harrow because I used to say what I thought.”
Yes, that and having sex with two girls at a school ball, I say.
Let’s pick up his life again at Billie Piper’s arrival into it. In their divorce, she accused him of unreasonable behaviour in their marriage, a concept he says is “a bit backward” while refusing to say whether, in his case, the allegation was true. His mother, he says, always said it took “two to tango”, but he does not want to talk about Piper or their custody fight (their sons’ custody is now shared). “I don’t have a bad word to say. She’s their mother.”
During this dark period he was prescribed sleeping pills, which did little good. He talked in one interview of having become suicidal. He says to me that in the old days people talked of mental breakdowns. Is that what he had?
“No. I’m too tough for that sort of thing. I’m sensitive though. So it’s an interesting combination. I’m profoundly sensitive but I’m also someone who won’t be bullied into submission.”
He won’t tell me if he has a girlfriend, but insists he is happy, confusingly adding that he has never not been. I explain why I am asking: people are looking at what is going on with this Reclaim thing and wondering if his life has got so screwed up that he has gone slightly mad.
“And they have the absolute right to say it. I think you can say whatever you want.”
He knows what I’m asking: I’m asking what kind of place he is in right now, whether he’s fit to lead a national party, whether it is a good idea for him, never mind the country, to do so.
“I think for me it’s an important thing. I feel that life is a journey and, as I alluded earlier, I have faith. So I have faith that you end up in a position and that position is important and my job and my duty are to try to create more equality for people.”
There is a massive problem with Reclaim, of course. Well, many, but here’s the fundamental one: it is fighting the way people with power and influence think, but you cannot pass a law to make Britain less woke.
“I mean, deep down I would like to get rid of the [2010] Equality Act, because that’s where a lot of the protected characteristics come in,” he says. “I’m no great brains on legislation but I look into it and I hire and I consult with people as part of the growing of the party and the growing of what is essentially a movement at the moment rather than a party, but will eventually have the fangs to be a party should needs be.”
The thought of Reclaim getting its fangs into an election or by-election is pretty terrifying. He mentions Rotherham and, in his words, “the mass raping of white women by Muslim men” and “the total silencing of it”. It could, he thinks, be an example of Reclaim achieving something “in microcosm”.
I’m sorry, Laurence, I say. I can’t imagine anything worse than having a candidate from Reclaim standing in Rotherham.
“I didn’t say that’s what we’re going to do, did I though?”
He did not. I am not sure if there is a plan. It is next to certain, however, that this project will fail, just as most new parties fail in the end in this country, usually quickly.
“All political careers end in doom. Yeah. My job is very simple. It’s a very simple job. My job is to go, ‘The Overton window is over here. We need to shove it back in the middle.’ ”
Where Fox may be right is that some of our national institutions have presumed a cultural consensus, including on free speech itself, without having created that consensus. He rightly challenges me when I patronisingly say that I would not like to meet his followers. He reads me a touching letter from an experienced nurse, once married to a Ugandan, who says Fox is right both about the NHS and race relations. “These are the people that aren’t flag-shaggers,” he says. “These are the people that care deeply about our country.”
Yet towards the end of our conversation he starts repeating a Trumpian conspiracy theorist about the Antifa movement and calls the outgoing resident of the White House “the last bastion of stopping America becoming socialist”. I turn off my recorder. I say I don’t want to hear any more.
When he is not detonating thought-bombs that mainly go off in his own face, he remains rather charming. His candour is warming. He listens. He is generous. The first time we met he insisted on giving me a bottle of his wedding champagne. This time I leave with a very good bottle of red. I don’t think he thinks he is bribing me and indeed, when he rings me the next day asking me to keep something out of the piece and I refuse, he peaceably accepts the fact.
He looks exhilarated but I’d say his is the exhilaration of someone who has thrown himself naked into the ocean in December.
He will soon realise it is bloody cold and there are sharks about. He texts me to say he hopes he expressed the importance of his desire to bring people together: “There is room for a positive message, even when we don’t agree.” Sure there is, but that is not why Paul the bodyguard is now in his life. Fox wants to shake things up. Let’s hope nothing worse than a milkshake gets spilt.

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Why Sasha Swire regrets nothing about Diary of an MP’s Wife
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Publish a political diary about the Tories in power and sit back and watch an entire colony of nose-diving gannets try to skewer a single shrimp astray from its shoal.
Gosh, the stuff that was written about me! Apparently I am, among other things of course, a frustrated housewife, a flesh-eating sexaholic (which came as news to my husband, I can tell you), a Lady Macbeth, a Becky Sharp figure, a member of the Devil’s Generation (Thatcher), a failed It girl and cabinet wannabe, an anti-Semite, a traitor, a vulgarian.
The headlines that festooned the Mail’s pages were particularly colourful and flapping in the winds of publication. I was even dispatched by its favourite columnist, Sarah not so Di Vine (as my husband calls her), to social Siberia, which was kind of OK because that was where everyone else was hanging out at the time as well.
● Extract one: ‘The PM starts to make lots of dogging jokes...’● Extract two: Dinners at Chequers, bodysurfing with David Cameron● Extract three: Negronis at dawn and Cameron’s last days● Decca Aitkenhead’s interview with Sasha Swire
The criticisms of my mostly unknown character, based on a few skimpy extracts and two interviews with journalists, came like cudgels trying to hammer a peg back into a small hole. Much criticism from the pursed lips of my own side as well: why wasn’t this woman censured? How did we not get to see her book before it went to print? How dare she espouse views so publicly other than our own official ones? What a supreme act of betrayal. Why didn’t her husband stop her? She was only a wife after all.
And there’s the rub. My observations as a wife were always going to be different from those written by former senior politicians, but they are no less worthy for it. And to be frank if you want a supersized serving of legacy bullshit, get down to your nearest independent bookshop to buy their great tomes. Although I wouldn’t recommend any by Old Ma May or her advisers, because you might just need electric shock therapy to revive you afterwards. No, you won’t get any of that from me, because I never had any need for self-vindication. Other than what I’m doing here, of course.
My diary is an altogether different sort of beast. The subtitle Inside and Outside Power gives the hint: I was sufficiently an insider to give the reader revealing moments and sufficiently an outsider to view everyone and everything with what one reviewer described as a “gimlet-eyed gaze”. I saw these people socially in their “off” moments, not when they were trying to make difficult decisions on important matters of state. I like to think I humanised them, softened their edges a little.
Because really, people don’t have a very high opinion of politicians at the best of times, do they? Out of necessity, they constantly need to remind voters that they are actually just LIKE US. They usually do this by standing by an oven, or a fridge, with the wife’s legs crossed and draped over a unit wearing a neatly ironed dress. Remember the Human Hedgehog, as I call him in the diary, James Brokenshire, mouthing off about building homes for young people, but all anyone noticed was that he had four ovens.
“I hate it when, come Christmas, there’s not enough room in the oven,” his innocent wife, Cathy, said, who also happened to have two dishwashers as well. Well, lucky her! Remember how Ed Miliband had two kitchens, but we only got to see the small galley Marxist one. And how about Dom Raab’s hard granite surfaces?
If we think politicians are different it is because we try to hold them to higher standards than we do ourselves, which is unfair and unworkable, and it usually ends in tears. Yes, dear reader, they are LIKE US. They can be childish and tell silly jokes, let off steam in salty Cornish waters; no soufflé pudding ever rose as much as some of their egos. They can be foolish and vain, duplicitous and ambitious. JUST LIKE US. And for those looking in the mirror only to see a different image coming back at them, well, I might have even done them something of a service.
Then there was the general assumption that I must have shed friends as quick as a redhead’s skin on a Marbella sunlounger. I’d like to say here I have not received a single letter of complaint, phone call or text from any politician or friend. So they are either complete cowards stewing in some hole somewhere or really not that bothered. And if they are stewing in a hole, they need to remember I have a whole decade of diaries before this one, so they should try to be nice to me. But probably easier for my conscience if they are not.
In fact, Sarah not so Di Vine’s husband, Michael Gove, who probably comes out of my diary the worst, had dinner with my husband, Hugo, after reading my book and told him how he found it, in parts, profoundly moving. Politicians as a rule usually come with a Teflon coating – not much sticks to them for long – and Michael is definitely a fine, shining example of this.
Interestingly, nearly all congratulatory texts/Whatsapp messages – and, yes, there were many – went straight to my husband’s mobile, naturally, because he is my guardian and keeper. Some even had the cheek to write, “I really enjoyed your book, Hugo.”
As for all that hoo-ha about David Cameron wanting to push me in the bushes to “give me one”. It was a joke, a J-O-K-E, everyone. He had his wife, whom he adores, three security guards and my husband behind him, so even if he wanted to do it, which he didn’t, it would have been quite a challenge, even for him. Samantha’s negroni at dawn? You’d be steeling yourself with one of those as well if you were leaving No 10 under the full blinding glare of the world’s media. The bitterer the better. Theresa May might have got Brexit done if she’d had a few.
Moving on to the assaults on my Tory friends: variations on a theme, mostly on us all having “a sense of self-entitlement” or being “elitists”. The full-on inverse snobbery from left-leaning hacks felt like a highly accelerated, rubber-burning, backward drive ending in several spectacular spinouts. Why is it acceptable to attack someone based on background, rich or poor? All it does is characterise a different sort of prejudice, surely? Could it be a symptom of their own social insecurity? An ego defence against the status claims of others?
I particularly enjoyed this pompous, intellectually pretentious comment in an upmarket literary paper about me being trained “through a key-stage programme of class shibboleths which then became wholly redundant, if not actively reprehensible, in their teenage years, but which they can’t shake as adults – resulting in a furtive and semi-hysterical preoccupation with the freemasonry of the upper class”. What the hell does that even mean? The writer of this particular review, who hurled out her stones from her northern castle, rents out her estate for shooting to rich City types, lives in one of the grandest and oldest houses in Chelsea and has added the word “aristocrat” to her biog on her publisher’s website. Lack of self-awareness? Moi? Hypocrisy was sprouting everywhere I can tell you.
What I do come from is a long line of politicians, vicars, doctors, soldiers and governors of faraway lands and foreign partisan fighters who have died in concentration camps for helping others escape tyranny. My mother, Miloska, is Slovenian and my grandfather died in Dachau along with other partisans. Miloska clambered over mountains to save other foreign women from genocide and rape during the Bosnian war, and she has built homes and schools for returning refugees in Srebrenica. I come from the sort of people who have obituaries in papers for services to others. Politics matters to my family, not as a means to lord it over anyone but as a means of making people equal, as a means of challenging human rights abuses.
Ultimately, politics is what I know; it’s what moves me. I suspect if I came from Scotland I would probably fight for independence. If I were Irish, I would have burnt out the Brits. If I were young, I would have glued myself to an underground train as a member of Extinction Rebellion. Instead I have beehives and a flower meadow.
I was not the traditional, old-fashioned and frustrated Tory wife as depicted. I was a modern woman who made the choice to make her home her office so she could watch her children grow; a lockdown-lover before her time if you like. I never had any desire to be in the limelight, which is why I have found this attention at times more than trying. I flirted briefly with the idea of becoming a politician but quickly realised it was not for me. This is who I am and who I always was, and who I always will be, merely a minor observer of people and their habits, a writer.
The other thing that brought out the heavy artillery was the notion of being immersed in a Cameron “chumocracy”. Anyone with a basic understanding of politics will know there are chumocracies in every government; it’s actually how they function. The closer the tribe is, the more efficient the machine runs. No loyalists and you have near-anarchy. Tony Blair was always appointing his friends to positions of power: Lord Falconer was a former flatmate; Anji Hunter was a childhood friend. He even put 176 of his “people” into the House of Lords. Winston Churchill had Brendan Bracken, Lord Lindemann and assorted others. James Callaghan sent his son-in-law, Peter Jay, to Washington as an ambassador. Each political chapter creates new elites which are there to propagate the new spirit of the age, usually gaining power by being anti the current establishment.
In truth, Cameron’s chumocracy actually comprised people from all backgrounds and ethnicities and those he had met on the political circuit, not just anyone he went to school or shot pheasants with. He even shafted my husband from his first shadow cabinet when he was rebranding the party because he didn’t want there to be too many people like him and George Osborne in it. And to you, George, that was not why I wrote and published the diary, as you suggested, for revenge. I wrote the diary because I’ve always written a diary, certainly not with an eye for publication, which is why over half of it had to be binned by the lawyers. It should be viewed as nothing more than a dangerous habit.
In the end, the electorate liked Cameron’s political philosophy. And they couldn’t have minded the Etonian thing that much because in the past ten years they have elected two of them and the Conservatives have won four elections. Class warfare doesn’t work; it didn’t work for Miliband and it didn’t work for Corbyn and it certainly won’t work for Keir Starmer. Labouring the issue will just lead to them getting gazumped at the finishing line all over again.
So yes, I found a lot of the commentary lazy, clichéd even. The decade that my diary covers was actually a period of profound social change in Britain; mass immigration, rising ethnic diversity and the expansion of higher education, culminating of course in Brexit. My diary might be mostly gossip-driven, tongue-in-cheek, elaborate pillow talk, but it needs to be seen against that backdrop, against a period when tribes were splintering and new ones were being formed. Of world orders realigning and authoritarian regimes expanding their power and reach. Because, really, Britain is just a mongrel of tribes, old and new, from near and far away. It is made up of many identities and beliefs. No creature is better than any other, nor is any grouping. No one gets to govern unless they have earned that right at the ballot box. There is no definitive version, we all have our own stories; they are just different in the telling, and this one just happens to be mine.
Last, but by no means least, the thorny issue of “betrayal”. So here I have to be honest with myself and say yes, I have gone places where most angels fear to tread. I have no excuses other than a good diarist needs to ignore the niceties of society and have a “complete inability to self-censor”, as Sarah not so Di Vine so cleverly put it of me. A diarist is a secret fifth columnist and sacrifices will have to be made to paint a portrait of his or her times.
I’m certainly not the first to intertwine gossip with affairs of state; how about Samuel Pepys? Churchill forbade his staff to keep diaries but if they hadn’t, we wouldn’t have got such a rounded portrait of the man. Sir Henry “Chips” Channon, arguably the foremost social and political diarist of mid-20th century Britain and whose unexpurgated diaries are shortly to be published, said, “What is more dull than a discreet diary?” How right he was.
For the chronicler herself, there is an almost inherent sense of duty in the act of writing everything down, an urgency to rescue events from oblivion. Hindsight is never as exciting as writing done in “real time”.
Moreover, loyalty in politics is not a simple virtue because of its fluid nature. Loyalty to one group or idea – in the case of divided loyalties – can often lead to the betrayal of some other value or group or person or brand.
During Brexit, for example, we saw the collapse of cabinet responsibility with ministers like Amber Rudd actually going against a government she was a member of. One of her supporters is even going around calling my husband and me “traitors”, which is a bit rich considering he was suspended from the Conservative Party and lost the whip for actively working against his prime minister and government. In fairness to them both, it is very difficult to keep allegiance in UK politics solidified. Everyone is shooting off to join different factions the whole time; it’s the nature of the beast – friendships are forever being tested and reworked. Hannah Arendt, a commentator on totalitarian regimes, wrote, “Total loyalty is possible only when fidelity is emptied of all concrete content, from which changes of mind might naturally arise.”
I would also say nearly everything in this diary is already public record. The problem is I bring the audience into the room so that it often reads like drama, fiction even, and that is not how people receive their information. They receive their news stories as bare bones, as facts and through legacy tomes, so a diary format is a much more inviting prospect for the reader; less so, I concede, for the characters portrayed.
Regrets, I have a few, but nothing major. I regret that my husband comes across as a bit hapless, which he isn’t at all in his professional life. It was much more a case of a husband coming home from his grand job in the capital and his wife telling him to take out the rubbish and the whole of the bottom of the sack spills out over the kitchen floor. As the Johann Wolfgang von Goethe quote goes, “No man is a hero to his valet. This is not because the hero is not a hero, but because the valet is a valet.” Because isn’t every husband hapless to his long-suffering wife? My husband and I share a great sense of the absurd. We have never taken ourselves too seriously, unlike many in politics. The truth is he achieved much as a minister and a constituency MP, but no one would be interested in me relaying the details of that, now would they?
Am I still writing a diary? Of course, I am. 2020 has been a fascinating year, personally and politically. Historians won’t study this time for another 30 years. Then they will have the transcripts from press conferences, the boffins’ opinions, the data, the inquiry conclusions, but how will we know what it actually felt like to live through it?
That is why oral histories and personal journeys are crucial to history. What did we do, how did we feel, who survived, who didn’t, what did we cook, what were the tensions in the home? Social media is excellent in gauging instantaneous reaction to events, but it all goes up in a puff of smoke. Digital long-term preservation is a real issue.
Everyone should be writing a diary. We all need to record, share and preserve the stories of our lives, of our times. No other historical document beats it. So there.

https://www.thetimes.com/world/us-world/.text:
In making this edit for this annual photography feature I was reminded of what an interesting year the past one has been and how fortunate and privileged I am to be in a position to document these global events for The Times. This year, 2020, dominated by Covid-19, has been more ‘interesting’ than most albeit for the wrong reasons.
We have seen our emergency services stretched, lived through a lockdown or two; the Prime Minister was admitted to hospital suffering from Covid-19 and there was widespread panic-buying of toilet roll. Unfortunately, many have been infected and tragically many have lost loved ones.
We are asked to choose our personal selection of photographs of the year and there have been several professional highlights such as an opportunity to travel to the US to document the recent election as I did in 2016, and being given rare access to an NHS hospital, the Royal Free in London, in April at the height of the pandemic.
Photographing during the pandemic has been challenging, not least of all because it is has been difficult to illustrate. During the first lockdown very few people were around. It was a surreal period. I became fascinated with facemasks as a symbol. At the same time, there were a number of protests — Black Lives Matter, Extinction Rebellion and anti-lockdown protests — and in covering these demonstrations social distancing became a moot point.
Above all I am grateful that we were able to carry on working out and about and show through photographs what was happening our readers. I hope you may find something in this selection that appeals.
I would also like to take this opportunity to thank all my colleagues for their support and patience this year.

image.caption: Katie Wood, a physiotherapist, talks to a patient on the “red ward” for Covid-only patients at the Royal Free in London
Putting on PPE is quite a process: members of staff in the “donning” area before entering the Covid ward

I have often found that the most dramatic picture appears within the first few moments of arriving at a place. This may be because senses are heightened and the benign gets greater attention than it would otherwise. That can be the only logical explanation. However, within seconds of arriving in the ICU at the Royal Free hospital, I saw this note being held up at the window of a cubicle while there reporting on how the hospital, its staff and patients were coping with Covid-19. Instinct rather than tact kicked in. There are no do overs in photography

A lone cyclist raises his arms for the camera as he cycles through Bank shortly after the nation was ordered to stay at home in late March. The view, looking towards the Royal Exchange, centre, and the Bank of England, left, would normally have been full of commuters on their way to work at this time of day
The actor John Boyega, centre, taking part in a Black Lives Matter protest outside the Houses of Parliament in June

Another photograph from the same protest in June. This time a policeofficer takes a knee in solidarity as a crowd gathered at the entrance to Downing Street. He wasn’t the only one but the only one I was able to photograph
Thousands of knot lift off from their temporary roost on a lagoon at Snettisham RSPB reserve in Norfolk

An HS2 protester is arrested after being brought down from a tree camp in Jones' Hill Wood. The ancient site near Great Missenden - now an HS2 construction site — is thought to be the wood that featured in Roald Dahl’s The Fantastic Mr Fox

Nigel Farage was in typically ebullient mood as he showed off his Union Jack patterned socks to the public gallery in the European parliament Council chamber on the day the UK formally left the European Union
Big crowds came to see President Trump address a rally in Reading, Pennsylvania, at the end of October. And again, this time, I’m sure he’s pointing at me as a member of the “fake news media”
President Trump disembarks from Air Force One to be greeted by a large crowd at Reading airport in the key state of Pennsylvania where both candidates campaigned heavily

This picture shows the palpable discord between the opposing sets of Trump and Biden supporters outside the Philadelphia convention centre as Pennsylvania’s votes were counted. One protester took his pet along in a backpack — although he didn’t let the cat out of the bag
Voters queued around the block in Littletown, Delaware, and across the US to secure a record turnout

Red deer in Richmond park just after dawn. Knowing the park reasonably well means that locating the deer is usually straightforward. Making an interesting picture is another matter. The cold temperature and the backlighting have given the impression (to me at least) that this deer is breathing out fire
A man, now in commonplace PPE, takes a moment at the southern end of Westminster Bridge outside St Thomas’ hospital, facing the Houses of Parliament, before continuing on his journey
Biden supporters celebrating outside the Convention Centre in Philadelphia after the result was declared last month
